intro: Every sport leaves paper behind. A newspaper notice announces a game. A club prints its rules. A league writes a charter that says who may join. A governor general buys a trophy and names trustees. Years later, a museum decides which objects to keep and which names to honor. Historians read all of these to learn what happened and who was left out.

This unit follows one sport, ice hockey, from painted Dutch canals and Mi'kmaq-carved sticks to the National Hockey League, the Colored Hockey League of Nova Scotia and the first women's Olympic tournament. Then it turns to objects and places: a stolen World Cup trophy, a gold medal made mostly of silver, a home plate marker in a Chicago parking lot, and the halls of fame and research groups that keep the record.

By the end, you can trace one sport through its documents and dates. You can tell a primary source from a later legend. You can explain how trophies, ballpark plans and archives shape memory. You can build an argument about a sport's past and name the record behind every claim.
bigQuestion: Who writes a sport's history, and how can we test their papers, objects and places against the record?

timeline.t: Pittsfield, Massachusetts, bans ball games, including baseball, near its meeting house
An organized hockey game is played at Montreal's Victoria Skating Rink
Lord Stanley buys a silver bowl as a challenge trophy for amateur hockey
The Colored Hockey League of the Maritimes is founded in Nova Scotia
The Mills Commission names Abner Doubleday as baseball's inventor
Owners found the National Hockey League in a Montreal hotel
The National Baseball Hall of Fame opens in Cooperstown, New York
The Jules Rimet Trophy is stolen in London and found by a dog
Researchers found the Society for American Baseball Research
Wrigley Field hosts its first completed night game
Women's ice hockey joins the Olympics at Nagano
Naismith's original basketball rules are sold at auction

words.d: a record made at the time of an event, such as a newspaper report printed the next day
a story that gives something a single inventor, place and birthday, often without good evidence
a founding document that sets up an organization and says who belongs
a prize the holder must defend against qualified challengers
the right, sold by a league, to own and run a team in a city
a barrier, often unwritten, that kept Black athletes out of white teams and leagues
a rule that exempts people already in a group from a new requirement
an object made by people that historians study for what it shows about the past
the record of who owned an object and when, used to show it is genuine
a measured drawing showing where a building sits on its piece of land
city rules about how land in each area may be used
a collection of old documents and records kept for study

test.q: Why is the March 3, 1875, Montreal game important to historians?
choices: It was the first game ever played on ice
It was announced and reported in print at the time
test.why: The Montreal Gazette's notice and report make it a well-documented organized game.

test.q: What did Lord Stanley give in 1892?
choices: A silver bowl as a challenge trophy
test.why: He bought a silver bowl as a challenge trophy for Canada's best amateur club.

test.q: Why was the NHL founded in 1917?
choices: Partly to shut out Toronto owner Eddie Livingstone
test.why: Owners formed a new league without Livingstone instead of expelling him.

test.q: What was the Colored Hockey League of the Maritimes?
choices: A league of Black teams in Nova Scotia founded in 1895
test.why: Black players and community leaders founded it in 1895 when white leagues shut them out.

test.q: When did women's ice hockey join the Olympics?
test.why: Women's hockey joined the Olympic program at Nagano in 1998.

test.q: What pushed the NHL toward its 1979 helmet rule?
choices: Calls for head protection after Bill Masterton's death in 1968
test.why: Masterton's death after a head injury in a game led to calls for helmets.

test.q: What evidence weakens the Doubleday story?
choices: Doubleday was a West Point cadet in 1839 and never wrote about baseball
The Mills report was never published
test.why: Doubleday's own record places him at West Point and never mentions baseball.

test.q: Who compiled the Olympic victor list that begins in 776 BCE?
test.why: Hippias of Elis compiled the list around 400 BCE.

test.q: The Webb Ellis plaque is best described as proof of what?
choices: That Webb Ellis wrote rugby's rules
That the Rugby Football Union began in 1823
What people later believed about rugby's origin
test.why: The story rests on an 1876 letter, so the plaque records a later belief.

test.q: Why did Brazil keep the Jules Rimet Trophy in 1970?
choices: It won the World Cup for the third time
test.why: FIFA's rule let the first three-time winner keep the trophy.

test.q: Which Games were the last to give solid gold medals?
test.why: After Stockholm 1912, gold medals became gold-plated silver.

test.q: What marks the site of the old Comiskey Park's home plate?
choices: A marble marker in a parking lot
test.why: The old park was torn down in 1991, and a marker in the lot shows where home plate stood.

test.q: What did Oriole Park at Camden Yards start in 1992?
test.why: Cities such as Cleveland, Denver and Pittsburgh copied its old-style design.

test.q: Why is the Pro Football Hall of Fame in Canton, Ohio?
choices: The league that became the NFL was founded there in 1920
It hosted the first Super Bowl
It won a vote of fans
test.why: The league was founded in a Canton car showroom in 1920.

test.q: What does an archive such as the LA84 Foundation's library do?
choices: Keeps old documents and records for study
test.why: Built with part of the 1984 Olympic surplus, its library keeps books and reports for researchers.

write.prompt: Choose one sport from this course. Did its governing bodies open their doors when their own documents say they did? Cite at least three dated records from this unit or earlier units, such as a charter, a rule change, a trophy's terms or a first roster, and explain what each shows.
tips: Name each record with its date and the body that made it.
Separate primary sources from later stories and legends.
Name who was shut out and the year a door opened.
Compare two institutions rather than judging one alone.
Use unit terms such as charter, provenance and color line.
